clue.text: Novel sort of attachment proposed by Moravia

definitions.text: Novel sort of attachment proposed by Moravia

parts.words: Novel sort of attachment proposed by Moravia
parts.note: Alberto Moravia wrote a novel about married love, so the bond in his title is the kind between spouses

explanation.surface: An unusual kind of affection suggested by the Italian novelist Moravia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as 'new', but it points to a book: Moravia's novel L'amore coniugale, translated into English as Conjugal Love.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the marriage bond, the attachment named in the title of Moravia's book.

clue.text: "Proud, fierce, jealous and irritable" Saxon

parts.note: these are the words Walter Scott uses for the Saxon thane, father to the hero, in Ivanhoe

explanation.surface: A quoted description of a hot-tempered Saxon.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's Ivanhoe gives this character sketch of the Saxon lord of Rotherwood, the hero's father.

clue.text: Unbalanced vernal poet

indicators.note: something unbalanced is out of order, so the letters of the next word are disordered

explanation.surface: A springtime poet who is not quite right in the head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unbalanced' rearranges VERNAL; Gérard de Nerval was a French Romantic poet who did suffer mental illness, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Gérard de Nerval was a nineteenth-century French poet.

clue.text: Very widely distributed, like Pope's prayer

explanation.surface: Something spread far and wide, as in a poem by Alexander Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander Pope wrote 'The Universal Prayer'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means found everywhere, and it is the adjective in the title of Pope's poem 'The Universal Prayer'.

clue.text: Scrupulous chap identified by Maugham and Eggleston

explanation.surface: An honest man recognised by two writers.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerset Maugham's first play and a novel by the American Edward Eggleston share this title.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of strict integrity is described by this phrase, which is also the title of works by Maugham and Eggleston.

clue.text: Poet showing connection between church and University Press, offered refusal to conform

parts.note: kirk is the Scottish word for a church
UP is the usual abbreviation for University Press, as in OUP

explanation.surface: A poet links a church with an academic publisher and refuses to fall in line.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing words describe the poet: James Kirkup was a conscientious objector in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: James Kirkup was an English poet and translator.

clue.text: Jones the architect says he's entering

explanation.surface: The architect Jones announces his arrival.
explanation.walkthrough: Inigo Jones was a seventeenth-century English architect; run together, 'in I go' is what someone entering says.
explanation.definitionFit: Inigo Jones designed the Banqueting House in Whitehall, and a person stepping inside might announce 'in I go'.

clue.text: Royal and ancient pathway for novelist

parts.note: royal can mean belonging to the king, the king's
a ley is a supposed ancient track linking landmarks

explanation.surface: A novelist follows a royal and ancient path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal and ancient' suggests the golf club at St Andrews, but the words split into the king's plus an old track.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Kingsley wrote The Water-Babies; Kingsley Amis is another novelist with the name.

clue.text: Motion put forward at Oxford

parts.note: the motion is a movement, the Oxford Movement led by Edward Pusey, not a debating proposal

explanation.surface: A proposal tabled at the Oxford Union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Motion' suggests a debating motion; it means a movement, the Oxford Movement, named after one of its leaders.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tractarian revival in the Church of England was nicknamed after its leader Edward Pusey.

clue.text: Hardy officer found Garland withheld

parts.note: in The Trumpet-Major the yeomanry officer Festus courts Anne Garland, who holds herself back from him

explanation.surface: A tough officer finds a wreath has been kept back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' is Thomas Hardy and 'Garland' is his heroine Anne Garland, not a wreath.
explanation.definitionFit: Festus is the boastful yeoman officer of Hardy's The Trumpet-Major whom Anne Garland rejects.

clue.text: Great literary figures like Gargantua and his son

explanation.surface: Major writers compared to Rabelais's characters.
explanation.walkthrough: Gargantua and his son Pantagruel are the giants of Rabelais.
explanation.definitionFit: Towering authors are called titans of literature, and Rabelais's Gargantua and Pantagruel are enormous creatures.

clue.text: What they all did for Sassoon in 1918

definitions.text: What they all did for Sassoon in 1918

parts.words: What they all did for Sassoon in 1918
parts.note: Siegfried Sassoon's poem of the Armistice describes the whole crowd bursting into song

explanation.surface: A question about what happened around Sassoon in 1918.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of Sassoon's 1919 poem celebrating the end of the Great War.

clue.text: Likeness that is cover for little review

indicators.note: the outer pair wraps around the next piece like a cover around a book

parts.note: IE is the abbreviation for id est, that is
a mag, short for magazine, is a little review

explanation.surface: A likeness used as the jacket for a small magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little review' is a small magazine, not a brief critique; 'that is' gives the Latin abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture or representation is a likeness of its subject.

clue.text: Clearly like Kipling's In Black and White

definitions.text: like Kipling's In Black and White

explanation.surface: Plainly, in the manner of a Kipling collection.
explanation.walkthrough: Something set down in black and white is plain to see.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means evidently, and something in black and white is stated beyond doubt.

clue.text: He restarts, we review sad Moore chronicle

indicators.note: to review is to go over again, here re-sorting the letters

explanation.surface: A man starts over as we look again at a sad book by Moore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'review' rearranges HE RESTARTS and WE.
explanation.definitionFit: George Moore's novel of a servant girl's hard life is titled after its heroine.

clue.text: From which Rex Warner's career took off?

definitions.text: From which Rex Warner's career took off?

parts.words: From which Rex Warner's career took off?
parts.note: the place planes take off from is also the title of Rex Warner's best-known novel

explanation.surface: A question about where Rex Warner's career was launched.
explanation.walkthrough: Rex Warner's 1941 novel is The Aerodrome.
explanation.definitionFit: An airfield is where aircraft depart, and it names Warner's novel.

clue.text: Beethoven song from South Australia

explanation.surface: A song by Beethoven coming from South Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: Beethoven's song 'Adelaide' shares its name with the state capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven set Matthisson's poem of that title, and the capital city of South Australia has the same name.

clue.text: Bumper edition of The Waves?

parts.note: a bumper edition is an enlarged one, so huge waves rather than Virginia Woolf's novel

explanation.surface: A special enlarged printing of Virginia Woolf's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Waves' looks like Woolf's novel; read literally, enormous waves.
explanation.definitionFit: Giant sea waves raised by earthquakes are the bumper version of ordinary waves.

clue.text: Sort of centuries-old historian led neurotics astray

indicators.note: letters gone astray have wandered out of their order

explanation.surface: An ancient historian leads anxious people off course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astray' rearranges LED NEUROTICS. Aubrey de Sélincourt translated Herodotus, so he is a 'sort of' ancient historian through his translation.
explanation.definitionFit: Aubrey de Sélincourt's Penguin translation made him the English voice of Herodotus, the historian from centuries ago.

clue.text: Last resort for Francesca

parts.note: Francesca's name ends with the town, a seaside resort, and she met her end there

explanation.surface: Francesca's final option.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last resort' is a final option; it is also the Adriatic resort in the name of Dante's Francesca, who was killed there.
explanation.definitionFit: Francesca da Rimini is named after the Italian seaside town.

clue.text: Dickens's powerful schoolmaster?

parts.note: the gentle headmaster in David Copperfield has a surname meaning powerful

explanation.surface: A forceful teacher in Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Strong of David Copperfield is in fact mild; the question mark marks the irony.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of Copperfield's kindly headmaster is an adjective for mighty.

clue.text: Position assumed by Miss Sobel

parts.note: Dava Sobel wrote a bestseller about measuring a ship's east-west position

explanation.surface: A stance taken by a woman named Sobel.
explanation.walkthrough: Dava Sobel's book tells how John Harrison solved the problem of east-west position at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: This coordinate fixes a position east or west, and is the title of Sobel's book.

clue.text: "— them in feign'd camps to real arms" (Matthew Prior)

definitions.text: "— them in feign'd camps to real arms" (Matthew Prior)

parts.words: "— them in feign'd camps to real arms" (Matthew Prior)
parts.note: the missing verb means to harden or accustom, training soldiers in mock camps for real war

explanation.surface: A line from Matthew Prior with its verb missing.
explanation.definitionFit: To accustom troops to hardship is to toughen them, the verb that fills the gap in Prior's line.

clue.text: Purport of James Hanley and Alan Jenkins

explanation.surface: The meaning behind two writers' works.
explanation.walkthrough: James Hanley's novel and Alan Jenkins's poetry collection share this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The general gist or meaning of something is its tenor, and both writers used the word as a title.

clue.text: A Morse foot

explanation.surface: A foot measured in Morse.
explanation.walkthrough: In Morse code the letter A is dot-dash, short then long, the pattern of this metrical foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A metrical foot of one short then one long syllable matches the dot-dash of A in Morse.

clue.text: Elizabeth Jolley's eponymous blonde

parts.note: the blonde is a cream-coloured horse giving its name to Jolley's novel

explanation.surface: A fair-haired woman who gives her name to an Elizabeth Jolley book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blonde' suggests a woman; it is a golden horse with a pale mane.
explanation.definitionFit: A golden horse with a white mane and tail is of this type, and Jolley's 1980 novel takes its name.

clue.text: Strindberg season

explanation.surface: A season of plays by Strindberg.
explanation.walkthrough: Strindberg wrote the play Easter (Påsk).
explanation.definitionFit: The spring Christian festival season names a Strindberg play.

clue.text: "I could never … be angry with his judgment for not — with me" (T. Browne, Religio Medici)

definitions.text: "I could never … be angry with his judgment for not — with me" (T. Browne, Religio Medici)

parts.words: "I could never … be angry with his judgment for not — with me" (T. Browne, Religio Medici)
parts.note: Browne says he never resents a man whose judgment differs from his, so the gap wants a word for concurring

explanation.surface: A line from Sir Thomas Browne with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Being of the same opinion as someone is the sense the gap in Browne's sentence needs.
